title: The flag and the wind
hook: two monks argue whether the flag or the wind moves; Huineng: your mind moves (Gateless Gate 29)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Juzhi's finger, and your line, your own finger. Did you answer one thing in your own words? Day two hundred eighty-two.

You know the argument that isn't really about the thing it's about. Two people at dinner, debating whether a movie was good, and twenty minutes later it's clearly about something else entirely. Both of them are sure they're right. Both of them are looking out, at the movie, at the other person. Neither is looking at what's happening inside. Picture a temple courtyard in southern China. A banner flaps on a pole in the wind. Two monks stand under it, arguing, and getting louder. A stranger is standing nearby, a lay worker from the south, and he's about to end the argument with one sentence.
screen: `THE ARGUMENT THAT ISN'T ABOUT THE THING.` → `A BANNER FLAPPING IN THE WIND.` → `TWO MONKS, GETTING LOUDER.`

segments.voice: One monk says: the flag is moving. The other says: no, the wind is moving. Back and forth. The stranger says: it isn't the wind moving, and it isn't the flag moving. Your minds are moving. The two monks were struck silent. The stranger was Huineng, remembered as the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, the Chinese school that became Zen. The Platform Sutra, the book of his teachings, tells this as the moment he was recognized: a poor, unlettered man from the south who had quietly received the robe and bowl of the Fifth Patriarch and had been hiding for years. The Gateless Gate keeps it as case twenty-nine. Now, Huineng isn't saying the flag is imaginary, or that wind doesn't exist. Look at what the monks were doing. Each had grabbed one side and was defending it. The movement that mattered was the grabbing: the mind flapping between flag and wind, mine and yours. Huineng turned their eyes around. And then Wumen, in his comment, turns it one more time. He says: it isn't the wind, it isn't the flag, and it isn't the mind. In his verse, wind, flag and mind moving are all the same mistake. Even your mind moves can become one more flag to argue about. The koan won't let you stand anywhere. What's left is just looking, before the arguing starts. Buddhists sometimes call that the mind that doesn't stick. Watch a flag and you'll see it.
screen: `FLAG OR WIND?` · `YOUR MINDS ARE MOVING.` · `HUINENG, THE SIXTH PATRIARCH.` · `NOT EVEN THE MIND.` · then, large: `MIND MOVES.`

segments.voice: Find something that moves: a curtain, a leaf outside, the steam from a cup, or simply your own belly as you breathe. Watch it. Notice how quickly the mind adds commentary: it's windy, I like that, I should close the window. Each time, come back to just the movement. Then notice the mind itself moving, thought after thought, and watch that the same way, like a flag in the wind. The bell holds the time.
The flag and the wind. Two monks argued which one moved; Huineng said, your minds are moving.
screen: `THE FLAG AND THE WIND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: mind moves. Today, in the middle of one disagreement, pause and notice what your own mind is doing before you answer. Day two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Zen communities honor Huineng as the Sixth Patriarch and study the Platform Sutra, which tells the flag-and-wind story; teachers use the koan to turn students' attention from outside arguments to the mind itself.

match.prompt: match each voice in the story.

myth: Huineng says the flag is imaginary
he turns the monks' attention to their own grasping, not away from the world.
the Platform Sutra tells this as the moment Huineng was recognized
a poor man from the south who had received the Fifth Patriarch's robe.
Wumen's verse calls wind, flag and mind moving the same mistake
even 'mind moves' can become one more flag to argue about.

fork.setup: two monks under a flapping banner are arguing: flag or wind? they turn to you. you're Huineng. what do you say?
options: not the wind, not the flag: your minds are moving.
fork.reveal: Huineng's answer silenced them, and Wumen later pushed further: not even the mind.

original.note: Chinese xīn dòng: the mind moves, the end of Huineng's answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Huineng was saying the world is all in your head.
what it means: the movement that mattered was the monks' grabbing at one side.
what a scholar hears: the Platform Sutra's story is set at a Guangzhou temple during a lecture on the Nirvana Sutra, though scholars debate how much of Huineng's life story is later legend.

sources.ref: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), case 29 and Wumen's comment and verse
Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (Liuzu tanjing)

notes: Case 29 and Wumen's comment/verse paraphrased: confirm Wumen's 'not the wind, not the flag, not the mind' reading.
The flag story's placement in the Platform Sutra: it appears in later (Zongbao) editions, not the Dunhuang version; confirm.
Huineng's 'years in hiding' after receiving the robe (traditionally about fifteen years): given without a number.
Trapdoor: Faxing temple in Guangzhou and the Nirvana Sutra lecture by Yinzong: confirm.
